works.title: The Invocation
works.note: The epic opens: Milton names his subject — the Fall — and calls on the Heavenly Muse to sing 'things unattempted yet in prose or rhyme,' and to justify the ways of God to men.

works.title: The Mind Is Its Own Place
works.source: Paradise Lost, Book I — Satan's defiance
works.note: Cast into Hell, Satan refuses despair: the mind can make a Heaven of Hell, and it is 'better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven.'

works.title: Hail, Holy Light
works.source: Paradise Lost, Book III — the invocation to Light
works.note: Blind, Milton turns to address Light itself, mourning the sight he has lost and asking the Celestial Light to shine inward — that he may tell of things invisible to mortal sight.

works.title: On the Liberty of Books
works.source: Areopagitica — A Speech for the Liberty of Unlicensed Printing
works.note: His foundational defense of free expression: to destroy a good book is to kill reason itself, for a book is 'the precious life-blood of a master spirit.'

works.title: On His Blindness
works.source: Sonnet XIX — 'When I consider how my light is spent'
works.note: Reckoning with his blindness, the poet fears his one talent now lies useless — until Patience answers that God needs no man's work: 'They also serve who only stand and wait.'

works.title: Fame Is the Spur
works.note: In his elegy for a drowned friend, Milton confronts the lure of fame — 'that last infirmity of noble mind' — and Phoebus's reply that true fame is judged not on earth but in Heaven.
